dx: Sydenham chorea in acute rheumatic fever
case: A 9-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of clumsiness and involuntary movements for 2 weeks. She drops objects, her handwriting has worsened, and she cries easily. About 3 months ago she had a sore throat with fever that was not treated. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg. Examination shows brief, irregular, nonrhythmic movements of the face, arms, and hands that stop during sleep. Her grip on the examiner's fingers alternately tightens and relaxes, and she cannot keep her tongue protruded. There is no rash, joint swelling, or heart murmur. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 14 mm/h (0 to 20). The antistreptolysin O titer is 180 Todd units (less than 200), and the anti-DNase B titer is elevated. Echocardiography and an MRI of the brain are normal. Diagnosis: Sydenham chorea in acute rheumatic fever.

questions.stem: Sydenham chorea is one major Jones criterion. Which of the following additional findings, if it develops, would count as a second major criterion?
options: PR interval of 0.22 seconds (0.10 to 0.18)
Temperature of 38.6 °C (101.5 °F)
Evanescent annular erythema on the trunk
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 64 mm/h
approach: List the five major Jones criteria: migratory polyarthritis, carditis, subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum, and Sydenham chorea.
Recognize a fleeting ring-shaped rash on the trunk as erythema marginatum.
Sort the rest: fever, a high ESR or CRP, and a prolonged PR interval are minor criteria even though they are common.
questions.why: Erythema marginatum is a pink rash of rings with pale centers on the trunk and proximal limbs. It comes and goes over hours and does not itch. It is one of the five major Jones criteria, so together with chorea it would give two major criteria. Chorea often appears months after the throat infection, which is why her ASO titer has already fallen while the anti-DNase B titer, which stays up longer, is still elevated.
whyNot: A prolonged PR interval is a minor criterion. Carditis, the major criterion, needs evidence of valve or heart muscle involvement, such as mitral regurgitation on echocardiography.
Fever is a minor criterion. It is common in acute rheumatic fever but is nonspecific.
Correct.
A raised ESR or CRP is a minor criterion. These acute phase markers are often normal in isolated chorea because chorea appears late, after the inflammation of the acute attack has settled.

topics: Timing of Sydenham chorea after strep infection

questions.stem: Which of the following mechanisms most likely explains her involuntary movements?
options: Antibodies to streptococcal antigens binding basal ganglia neurons
Immune complexes of streptococcal antigen deposited in cerebral vessels
Superantigen activation of T cells infiltrating the cerebral cortex
Persistent streptococcal infection of the caudate nucleus
approach: Note the timing: chorea months after an untreated strep throat, with sterile tissues and no fever.
Rheumatic fever is molecular mimicry: antibodies made against streptococcal antigens bind similar host proteins.
Antibody binding to antigens on host cells is type II hypersensitivity, so look for antibodies acting on the neurons that control movement.
questions.why: Sydenham chorea is caused by molecular mimicry. Antibodies made against group A streptococcal antigens cross-react with neurons of the basal ganglia, mainly the caudate and putamen, and disturb their signaling. Because antibodies bind antigens on host cells, this is type II hypersensitivity, the same mechanism by which antibodies to M protein injure the heart in rheumatic carditis. No organisms are present in the brain, and the chorea usually resolves over weeks to months.
whyNot: Correct.
Immune complex deposition is type III hypersensitivity. It explains poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. Rheumatic fever is driven by antibodies to cross-reactive host cell antigens.
Streptococcal superantigens cause the scarlet fever rash and streptococcal toxic shock during active infection. They do not cause a delayed autoimmune disease months later.
Rheumatic fever is sterile and immune-mediated, and there is no infection in the brain or heart. Antibiotics are given to clear any remaining throat carriage and to prevent recurrences.

questions.stem: The streptococcal surface protein whose resemblance to cardiac myosin drives rheumatic carditis also helped the organism survive in her pharynx. Which of the following was its main role in virulence?
options: Lysis of erythrocytes by oxygen-labile pore formation
Spread through tissue by degradation of hyaluronic acid
Dissolution of fibrin clots by activation of plasminogen
Resistance to phagocytosis by limiting C3b deposition
approach: Identify the surface protein that mimics cardiac myosin in rheumatic fever: M protein of Streptococcus pyogenes.
Recall what M protein does for the organism during infection.
Match each remaining option to its own streptococcal product (streptolysin O, hyaluronidase, streptokinase).
questions.why: M protein is the main virulence factor of Streptococcus pyogenes. It projects from the cell wall and binds host complement regulators such as factor H, so less C3b is deposited on the bacterium and neutrophils cannot ingest it well. Protective immunity comes from type-specific antibody to M protein, which restores opsonization. Parts of M protein resemble cardiac myosin and other host proteins, which is why the same antigen drives rheumatic carditis. The antibodies behind chorea cross-react mainly with basal ganglia antigens and the group A carbohydrate.
whyNot: This describes streptolysin O, the oxygen-labile hemolysin. Antibody to it (ASO) is a marker of recent streptococcal infection.
This describes hyaluronidase, a spreading factor that helps streptococci move through connective tissue in cellulitis.
This describes streptokinase, which converts plasminogen to plasmin and dissolves clots so the infection can spread.
Correct.

questions.stem: During her sore throat 3 months ago, which of the following lymph nodes was most likely enlarged and tender?
options: Submental nodes beneath the chin
Jugulodigastric node at the jaw angle
Occipital nodes at the base of the skull
Left supraclavicular node above the clavicle
approach: Identify the infected site: the palatine tonsils in streptococcal pharyngitis.
Recall the first node that drains the tonsils.
Rule out node groups that drain other regions of the head or the thoracic duct.
questions.why: The palatine tonsils drain mainly to the jugulodigastric (tonsillar) node. It is a deep cervical node just below the angle of the mandible, where the posterior belly of the digastric crosses the internal jugular vein. It becomes enlarged and tender in streptococcal pharyngitis, and tender anterior cervical nodes are one of the clinical clues to strep throat.
whyNot: Submental nodes drain the chin, the central lower lip, the tip of the tongue, and the floor of the mouth.
Correct.
Occipital nodes drain the back of the scalp. They enlarge with scalp infections and, with postauricular nodes, in rubella.
The left supraclavicular (Virchow) node lies near the end of the thoracic duct. Its enlargement suggests abdominal or thoracic cancer.

topics: Lymphatic drainage of the head and neck

dx: Menstrual toxic shock syndrome from Staphylococcus aureus TSST-1
case: A 19-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of fever, vomiting, watery diarrhea, and lightheadedness for 1 day. She is on day 4 of her menstrual period and has been using high-absorbency tampons. Temperature is 39.8 °C (103.6 °F), pulse is 132/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 78/42 mm Hg. Examination shows a diffuse, blanching, red macular rash, bilateral conjunctival injection, and a red oropharynx. A tampon is removed from the vagina. Leukocyte count is 17,800/mm3 (4,500 to 11,000), platelet count is 86,000/mm3 (150,000 to 400,000), serum creatinine is 2.3 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.1), and serum creatine kinase is 1,240 U/L (30 to 170). Blood cultures are negative. Vaginal culture grows Staphylococcus aureus that produces toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 (TSST-1). Diagnosis: menstrual toxic shock syndrome.

questions.stem: Her peripheral blood T cells are analyzed by flow cytometry during the first week of illness. Which of the following findings is most likely?
options: Expansion of one T cell clone with a single TCR
Expansion of T cells bearing one V-beta family
Expansion of gamma-delta T cells in the blood
Expansion of FOXP3-positive regulatory T cells
approach: Identify TSST-1 as a superantigen.
Recall where it binds: MHC class II and the V-beta region of the T cell receptor, outside the peptide groove.
Predict the result: every T cell using that V-beta segment is activated, whatever its antigen specificity.
questions.why: TSST-1 is a superantigen. It binds MHC class II on antigen-presenting cells and the V-beta region of the T cell receptor without being processed into peptide. Any T cell that uses a matching V-beta segment is activated, whatever peptide its receptor recognizes. For TSST-1 this is mainly V-beta 2, so up to about 20% of all T cells can be activated at once, compared with far less than 1% in a normal response to a peptide antigen. These many clones release IL-2, IFN-gamma, and TNF together, producing a cytokine storm.
whyNot: Expansion of a single clone with one TCR sequence suggests a T cell neoplasm. A superantigen activates many different clones at the same time.
Correct.
Gamma-delta T cells use gamma and delta chains and have no TCR beta chain, so they are not the target of a V-beta-binding superantigen.
Superantigens drive effector cytokine release. A rise in regulatory T cells would damp the response and does not explain the shock.

questions.stem: Activated T cells release IL-2 and interferon-gamma, which drive macrophages to release large amounts of TNF-alpha and IL-1. Which of the following effects of these cytokines most directly lowers her systemic vascular resistance?
options: Release of endothelin from endothelial cells
Release of vasopressin from the posterior pituitary
Synthesis of thromboxane A2 by activated platelets
Increased nitric oxide synthesis in arterioles
approach: Note that she meets SIRS criteria (temperature above 38 °C (100.4 °F), pulse above 90/min, respirations above 20/min, leukocytes above 12,000/mm3) and is hypotensive.
Low systemic vascular resistance means arteriolar dilation.
Pick the cytokine effect that dilates arterioles; the other options constrict them.
questions.why: TNF-alpha and IL-1 induce the inducible form of nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) in vascular smooth muscle and endothelium. Large amounts of nitric oxide raise cGMP in smooth muscle and relax arterioles, so systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure fall. The same cytokines make the endothelium leaky and procoagulant, which explains capillary leak and her falling platelet count. Gram-negative septic shock uses the same cytokine pathway, started instead by LPS binding CD14 and TLR4 on macrophages.
whyNot: Endothelin is a potent vasoconstrictor. It would raise systemic vascular resistance.
Vasopressin constricts arterioles through V1 receptors. Its release is a compensatory response to hypotension.
Thromboxane A2 constricts vessels and aggregates platelets. It would raise vascular resistance.
Correct.

questions.stem: Staphylococcus aureus in her vagina activates complement through the alternative pathway. Which of the following complement functions contributes most to clearing this organism?
options: Opsonization by C3b for neutrophil uptake
Lysis by the C5b-9 membrane attack complex
Clearance of immune complexes bound to erythrocytes
Mast cell degranulation induced by C3a
approach: Identify the organism as a gram-positive coccus with a thick peptidoglycan wall.
Recall that the membrane attack complex cannot reach the membrane of gram-positive bacteria.
Gram-positive bacteria are cleared by phagocytes, which need opsonins such as C3b.
questions.why: Gram-positive bacteria such as S aureus have a thick peptidoglycan wall that keeps the membrane attack complex from reaching the cell membrane. Their clearance depends on opsonization: C3b and IgG coat the bacterium, and neutrophils and macrophages ingest it through complement and Fc receptors. C5a adds neutrophil recruitment. The membrane attack complex matters most against Neisseria, which is why C5 to C9 deficiency causes recurrent neisserial infections.
whyNot: Correct.
The C5b-9 complex lyses gram-negative bacteria such as Neisseria. The thick peptidoglycan of S aureus blocks it.
C3b on immune complexes lets erythrocytes carry them to the liver and spleen through CR1. This clears soluble complexes, not whole bacteria.
C3a is an anaphylatoxin that releases histamine and raises vascular permeability. It promotes inflammation but does not let phagocytes ingest the organism.

questions.stem: Although TSST-1 bypasses peptide recognition, the T cells it engages still need a costimulatory signal to proliferate and secrete IL-2. Which of the following receptor and ligand pairs provides this signal?
options: CTLA-4 on T cells and B7 on the presenting cell
PD-1 on T cells and PD-L1 on the presenting cell
CD28 on T cells and B7 on the presenting cell
LFA-1 on T cells and ICAM-1 on the presenting cell
approach: Signal 1 here is the superantigen bridging MHC class II and the TCR.
Signal 2 is the costimulatory signal that triggers IL-2 production.
Separate the activating pair from the inhibitory pairs (CTLA-4, PD-1) and the adhesion pair (LFA-1 and ICAM-1).
questions.why: Full T cell activation needs two signals. Signal 1 is engagement of the T cell receptor, supplied here by the superantigen. Signal 2 is CD28 on the T cell binding B7-1 (CD80) or B7-2 (CD86) on the antigen-presenting cell, which drives IL-2 production and proliferation. TCR signaling without CD28 costimulation leads to anergy. CTLA-4 and PD-1 are inhibitory receptors that shut the response down later.
whyNot: CTLA-4 binds B7 more tightly than CD28 does, but it sends an inhibitory signal. CTLA-4-Ig (abatacept) is used to block costimulation.
PD-1 binding PD-L1 inhibits T cells. Tumors use PD-L1 to escape, and PD-1 blockers release this brake.
Correct.
LFA-1 binding ICAM-1 holds the T cell and the presenting cell together. It is an adhesion step, and the classic second signal for IL-2 is CD28 with B7.

dx: Dialysis-related beta2-microglobulin amyloidosis with carpal tunnel syndrome
case: A 61-year-old woman comes to the physician because of numbness and tingling of the thumb, index, and middle fingers of both hands for 8 months. The symptoms wake her at night, and she also has aching in both shoulders. She has received hemodialysis three times weekly for 15 years for end-stage kidney disease from autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. Temperature is 36.7 °C (98.1 °F), pulse is 76/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 142/86 mm Hg. Tapping over the volar wrists reproduces the paresthesias, and there is mild thenar atrophy. Wrist radiographs show cystic lucencies in the carpal bones. Serum beta2-microglobulin is 38 mg/L (1.2 to 2.7). Serum immunofixation shows no monoclonal protein. Tissue removed at carpal tunnel release stains with Congo red and reacts with antibody to beta2-microglobulin. Diagnosis: dialysis-related beta2-microglobulin amyloidosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why the precursor protein reached such a high serum concentration in this patient?
options: Overproduction by a clone of plasma cells
Increased hepatic synthesis driven by IL-6
Inherited mutation that destabilizes the protein
Loss of renal filtration and tubular breakdown
approach: Identify the amyloid protein from the immunostain: beta2-microglobulin.
Recall how this small protein is normally removed: glomerular filtration, then reabsorption and breakdown in the proximal tubule.
Match the setting: years of dialysis without kidney function, and conventional dialysis removes it poorly.
questions.why: Beta2-microglobulin is shed constantly from cell surfaces. It is small (about 12 kDa), so it is normally filtered freely by the glomerulus and then reabsorbed and broken down in the proximal tubule. In end-stage kidney disease this clearance is lost, and conventional dialysis membranes remove it poorly. After years of high levels the protein misfolds into amyloid that favors collagen-rich tissue: tenosynovium, joint capsules, and bone.
whyNot: A plasma cell clone produces light chains and AL amyloid. Her immunofixation shows no monoclonal protein.
IL-6 drives hepatic synthesis of serum amyloid A in chronic inflammation, which causes AA amyloidosis.
Inherited destabilizing mutations cause hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis. Her protein is normal in structure and simply builds up.
Correct.

topics: Amyloid protein types and their settings

questions.stem: Amyloid formed from this protein, from immunoglobulin light chains, and from serum amyloid A all show apple-green birefringence after Congo red staining. Which structural feature shared by all amyloid deposits explains this?
options: Alpha-helical coiled coils
Cross-beta-pleated sheet fibrils
Triple helices of collagen
Heavily glycosylated side chains
approach: Note that very different precursor proteins give the same staining pattern.
So the shared feature must be the misfolded structure, not the protein sequence.
Recall that amyloid fibrils are built from beta-pleated sheets.
questions.why: Every amyloid protein, whatever its source, misfolds into the same structure: rigid, nonbranching fibrils made of beta-pleated sheets stacked across the long axis of the fibril (cross-beta). Congo red lines up along these regular fibrils, so the stained deposit shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light. The same fibrils resist proteolysis, which is why the deposits build up in the extracellular space.
whyNot: Alpha-helical coiled coils make up proteins such as keratin and myosin. Amyloid formation is a shift away from helices toward beta sheets.
Correct.
Collagen forms triple helices. Amyloid often lies next to collagen, but its own fibrils are beta-sheet structures.
Heavy glycosylation is typical of mucins and proteoglycans, which stain with PAS or Alcian blue. It does not give Congo red birefringence.

questions.stem: In healthy tissue, the precursor of this amyloid is part of which of the following molecules?
options: MHC class II on antigen-presenting cells, recognized by CD4 T cells
The invariant chain occupying the class II peptide groove
MHC class I on all nucleated cells, recognized by CD8 T cells
The CD3 signaling complex of the T cell receptor
approach: Identify the precursor: beta2-microglobulin.
Recall which MHC molecule uses beta2-microglobulin as its light chain.
Link that molecule to its cell distribution and the T cells that recognize it.
questions.why: Beta2-microglobulin is the light chain of every MHC class I molecule. It pairs noncovalently with the polymorphic alpha heavy chain (HLA-A, -B, or -C), which forms the peptide groove. Class I is expressed on all nucleated cells and presents peptides made inside the cell to CD8 T cells. Because so many cells turn over class I, beta2-microglobulin enters the blood continuously, and the kidney is its main route of removal.
whyNot: MHC class II is built from an alpha and a beta chain that both cross the membrane. It has no beta2-microglobulin.
The invariant chain blocks the class II groove in the endoplasmic reticulum until it is cut down to CLIP and exchanged for peptide by HLA-DM. It is unrelated to beta2-microglobulin.
Correct.
CD3 chains carry signals from the T cell receptor into the cell. They do not contain beta2-microglobulin.

topics: MHC class I versus class II structure

questions.stem: Carpal tunnel syndrome can also result from primary (AL) amyloidosis. Which of the following additional findings in a patient receiving long-term dialysis would most strongly suggest AL amyloidosis instead?
options: Periorbital purpura with macroglossia
Destructive arthropathy of the cervical spine
Scapulohumeral periarthritis with shoulder pain
Bone cysts in the femoral neck
approach: Recall the pattern of dialysis-related amyloid: mostly bones, joints, and tendon sheaths.
Recall the pattern of AL amyloid: many organs, with soft-tissue signs from deposits in vessels and the tongue.
Pick the finding that dialysis-related amyloid does not typically produce.
questions.why: AL amyloid comes from monoclonal light chains made by a plasma cell clone. It deposits in many organs, including the heart, kidney, and nerves, and its soft-tissue clues are macroglossia and periorbital purpura, which comes from amyloid in small vessel walls that makes them fragile. Dialysis-related amyloid stays mostly in the musculoskeletal system: carpal tunnel syndrome, shoulder periarthritis, bone cysts, and destructive spondyloarthropathy. A serum free light chain assay or immunofixation would confirm the AL type.
whyNot: Correct.
Destructive spondyloarthropathy, often in the cervical spine, is a typical complication of dialysis-related amyloid.
Shoulder pain from amyloid in the rotator cuff and joint capsule is one of the most common features of dialysis-related amyloid.
Amyloid bone cysts in the carpal bones, femoral neck, and humeral head are typical of dialysis-related amyloid and can lead to pathologic fractures.

dx: Hydrops fetalis from maternal parvovirus B19 infection
case: A 29-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 22 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a follow-up ultrasound examination. About 4 weeks ago she had a low-grade fever, followed by painful swelling of the small joints of both hands that has since resolved. Her blood type is O, Rh-positive, and her red cell antibody screen is negative. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 84/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg. Ultrasound shows fetal ascites, pleural effusions, scalp edema, and a raised middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity, indicating fetal anemia. Serum parvovirus B19 IgM and IgG are positive. Cordocentesis shows a fetal hemoglobin of 3.9 g/dL (about 11 to 13 at this gestational age), a very low reticulocyte count, and a negative direct antiglobulin test. Diagnosis: hydrops fetalis from maternal parvovirus B19 infection.

questions.stem: Which of the following sequences best explains the fetal hydrops?
options: Erythroid aplasia, severe anemia, high-output cardiac failure
Maternal anti-D IgG, fetal hemolysis, high-output cardiac failure
Fetal hepatitis, hypoalbuminemia, reduced plasma oncotic pressure
Fetal thrombocytopenia, intracranial bleeding, hypovolemic shock
approach: Note the clues: severe fetal anemia with a very low reticulocyte count, a negative direct antiglobulin test, and an Rh-positive mother.
Low reticulocytes mean red cells are not being made, which fits parvovirus B19 infection of erythroid precursors.
Severe anemia forces cardiac output up until the heart fails, and fluid collects in body cavities and skin.
questions.why: Parvovirus B19 crosses the placenta and lytically infects fetal erythroid progenitors, which divide rapidly while fetal red cells have a short lifespan. Red cell production stops, and the fetus becomes severely anemic. Cardiac output rises to keep oxygen delivery up until the heart fails, venous pressure climbs, and fluid collects in the peritoneal and pleural spaces and the skin. Viral myocarditis can add to the heart failure. The Rh-positive mother, negative antibody screen, and negative direct antiglobulin test rule out alloimmune hemolysis.
whyNot: Correct.
Anti-D hemolytic disease needs an Rh-negative mother with anti-D antibody. Hemolysis would also give a positive direct antiglobulin test and a high reticulocyte count.
Low fetal albumin can add to hydrops, but it does not explain severe anemia with absent reticulocytes, which is the central lesion here.
Parvovirus can lower platelets, but bleeding with hypovolemic shock does not produce generalized edema and effusions.

questions.stem: The virus can replicate only in cells that are actively synthesizing DNA, such as dividing erythroid progenitors. Which feature of the virus best explains this requirement?
options: Large double-stranded DNA genome encoding its own polymerase
Segmented negative-sense RNA genome with a packaged polymerase
Small single-stranded DNA genome lacking a polymerase
Positive-sense RNA genome copied by a viral replicase
approach: Recall the structure of parvovirus B19: a small, nonenveloped virus with single-stranded DNA.
A virus too small to encode its own DNA polymerase must borrow the host's.
Host DNA polymerases are active only in S phase, so the virus needs dividing cells.
questions.why: Parvovirus B19 is one of the smallest DNA viruses: a nonenveloped icosahedral capsid around a single-stranded DNA genome of about 5.6 kb. It does not encode a DNA polymerase, so it depends on the host cell's replication machinery, which is active only in S phase. Dividing erythroid progenitors carry the P antigen receptor and supply the S-phase enzymes, so the virus kills them selectively and red cell production stops.
whyNot: Large double-stranded DNA viruses such as the herpesviruses encode their own DNA polymerase, so they can replicate in nondividing cells such as neurons.
A segmented negative-sense RNA genome with a packaged polymerase describes influenza virus, which replicates without host DNA synthesis.
Correct.
Positive-sense RNA viruses such as picornaviruses copy their genome with their own RNA polymerase in the cytoplasm and do not need host S phase.

questions.stem: Her 5-year-old son had a rash illness about 5 weeks ago and is the most likely source of her infection. Which of the following best describes his illness?
options: High fever for 3 days, then a truncal rash as the fever fell
Mild fever, then red cheeks and a lacy rash on the limbs
Cough and conjunctivitis, then a rash spreading from the hairline
Tender postauricular nodes with a pink rash spreading from the face
approach: Identify the virus that infected her: parvovirus B19, which in children causes erythema infectiosum.
Recall its course: a mild prodrome, then a slapped-cheek rash, then a lacy rash on the limbs.
Separate it from roseola, measles, and rubella by the rash pattern and its timing relative to fever.
questions.why: Erythema infectiosum begins with a mild, flulike prodrome. About a week later, bright red cheeks appear, followed by a lacy, reticular rash on the arms and legs that can fade and return for weeks. By the time the rash appears the child has made antibody and is no longer very contagious, so spread happens during the prodrome. Her own symmetric small-joint arthropathy is the usual adult presentation of the same infection.
whyNot: Several days of high fever followed by a truncal rash as the fever breaks is roseola from HHV-6 in children under 2 years.
Correct.
Cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis followed by a rash spreading from the hairline downward is measles.
A mild face-to-trunk rash with postauricular nodes is rubella. In pregnancy it causes cataracts, deafness, and patent ductus arteriosus rather than hydrops.

topics: Childhood exanthems by rash pattern and fever timing

questions.stem: Fetal serum albumin is within the reference range, and umbilical venous pressure is elevated. Which change in capillary Starling forces most directly increases fluid filtration into the fetal tissues?
options: Decreased plasma oncotic pressure
Increased interstitial hydrostatic pressure
Increased interstitial oncotic pressure
Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure
approach: List the Starling forces: capillary and interstitial hydrostatic pressure, plasma and interstitial oncotic pressure.
Normal albumin means plasma oncotic pressure is preserved.
Raised venous pressure is transmitted back to the capillaries, so capillary hydrostatic pressure rises.
questions.why: Net filtration depends mainly on capillary hydrostatic pressure pushing fluid out against plasma oncotic pressure holding it in, with interstitial pressures opposing each. Heart failure raises venous pressure, which is transmitted back into the capillaries and raises capillary hydrostatic pressure, so more fluid leaves the vessels. Normally the small net filtrate is returned to the blood as lymph, about 2 to 3 L per day in an adult. Edema forms when filtration outpaces lymph return, and high central venous pressure also slows lymph emptying into the veins.
whyNot: Plasma oncotic pressure depends mainly on albumin, which is normal here.
A rise in interstitial hydrostatic pressure opposes filtration. It is a result of fluid collecting in the tissues and acts as a safety factor against edema.
Interstitial oncotic pressure rises when capillaries leak protein. Raised venous pressure does not cause this, and lymph flow normally carries filtered protein away.
Correct.

dx: Haemophilus influenzae type b meningitis in an unvaccinated child with sickle cell disease
case: A 3-year-old boy with homozygous sickle cell disease (HbSS) is brought to the emergency department because of fever, vomiting, and increasing drowsiness for 1 day. His parents declined all childhood vaccinations, and he does not take penicillin prophylaxis. Temperature is 39.6 °C (103.3 °F), pulse is 156/min, respirations are 30/min, and blood pressure is 92/54 mm Hg. He is lethargic and irritable, with neck stiffness and a positive Kernig sign. The spleen is not palpable. Hemoglobin is 7.4 g/dL (11.5 to 13.5), and the blood smear shows sickled cells and Howell-Jolly bodies. Cerebrospinal fluid shows a leukocyte count of 2,600/mm3 (0 to 5) with 92% neutrophils, glucose of 16 mg/dL (40 to 70), and protein of 240 mg/dL (15 to 45). Gram stain shows small gram-negative coccobacilli, and culture grows Haemophilus influenzae type b. Diagnosis: Haemophilus influenzae type b meningitis.

questions.stem: Which of the following bacterial components most directly allows this organism to survive in his bloodstream and reach the meninges?
options: Secreted protease that cleaves IgA1
Adhesive pili binding respiratory epithelium
Polyribosylribitol phosphate capsule
Hyaluronic acid capsule resembling host tissue
approach: Separate the steps of invasion: colonizing the nasopharynx, then surviving in the blood.
Survival in the blood depends on resisting complement and phagocytosis, which is the job of a capsule.
Recall the composition of the type b capsule.
questions.why: The type b capsule is a polymer of ribose, ribitol, and phosphate (polyribosylribitol phosphate, PRP). It resists complement-mediated killing and phagocytosis, so the organism survives in the blood and seeds the meninges. Before the conjugate vaccine, type b caused nearly all invasive H influenzae disease in children, and antibody to PRP is what protects. IgA protease and pili help with the earlier step of colonizing the nasopharynx.
whyNot: IgA1 protease cleaves secretory IgA on mucosal surfaces and helps colonization. It does little to protect the organism in the bloodstream.
Pili help the organism attach to respiratory epithelium during colonization. They do not protect against complement and phagocytes in the blood.
Correct.
A hyaluronic acid capsule that mimics host tissue belongs to Streptococcus pyogenes, a gram-positive coccus.

questions.stem: In unvaccinated children without sickle cell disease, invasive disease from this organism is most common between about 6 months and 2 years of age. Which of the following best explains this age distribution?
options: Waning maternal IgG and poor anti-polysaccharide responses
Loss of breast milk secretory IgA after the child is weaned
Immature neutrophils that cannot generate an oxidative burst
Low thymic output of naive T cells during the first 2 years
approach: Ask what protects the youngest infants: maternal IgG that crossed the placenta.
Ask what protects older children: their own antibody to the capsule.
Children younger than about 2 years make weak T-independent responses to polysaccharides, leaving a gap between the two.
questions.why: Newborns are protected by maternal IgG to the type b capsule that crossed the placenta, and this antibody falls over the first months of life. Children younger than about 2 years respond poorly to polysaccharide antigens, which are T-independent and depend on B cell populations that are still immature. This leaves a window, roughly 6 months to 2 years, when the child has neither maternal nor his own antibody. Older children make anti-capsule antibody after natural exposure, while children with sickle cell disease stay at risk longer because they lack splenic clearance.
whyNot: Correct.
Breast milk IgA offers some mucosal protection, but invasive Hib disease also peaks in this age range in children who were never breastfed, and the key protection in blood is IgG.
Neutrophils in healthy infants make an oxidative burst. A failed burst is the defect of chronic granulomatous disease, which predisposes to catalase-positive organisms.
The thymus is largest and most active in infancy and early childhood, so naive T cell output is high at this age.

questions.stem: He is given catch-up doses of the Hib conjugate vaccine and the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine. Which of the following is a property of the Hib conjugate vaccine that the MMR vaccine lacks?
options: Induction of cytotoxic CD8 T cells against infected cells
Replication of the vaccine organism within the recipient
Induction of antibody against viral surface glycoproteins
Safe use in children with severe immunodeficiency
approach: Classify each vaccine: MMR is live attenuated; the Hib vaccine is a polysaccharide linked to a carrier protein.
Live vaccines replicate, reach the cytosol, and induce CD8 T cells and antibody.
A vaccine with nothing that can replicate cannot cause vaccine-strain infection in an immunodeficient host.
questions.why: MMR is a live attenuated vaccine. The weakened viruses replicate in the recipient, are processed in the cytosol and presented on MHC class I, and induce CD8 T cells and long-lasting antibody. Because they replicate, live vaccines can cause disseminated infection in severe immunodeficiency and are avoided there and in pregnancy. The Hib vaccine is a protein-conjugated polysaccharide with nothing that can replicate, so it carries no risk of vaccine-strain infection, though it may protect poorly in a child who cannot make antibody. Sickle cell disease is not a contraindication to live vaccines.
whyNot: Induction of CD8 T cells is a property of live vaccines like MMR, whose viral proteins are made inside host cells and shown on MHC class I.
Replication of the vaccine organism is what defines a live attenuated vaccine such as MMR.
MMR induces antibody against viral surface glycoproteins such as measles hemagglutinin. The Hib vaccine induces antibody against a bacterial capsule.
Correct.

topics: Live versus inactivated and conjugate vaccines

questions.stem: Without vaccination or prophylaxis, his loss of splenic function places him at greatest risk of overwhelming sepsis from which other organism?
options: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Streptococcus pneumoniae
Staphylococcus epidermidis
Listeria monocytogenes
approach: Recognize functional asplenia from sickle cell disease: Howell-Jolly bodies and a nonpalpable spleen.
Recall the spleen's role in clearing encapsulated bacteria from the blood.
Pick the encapsulated organism that most often causes overwhelming sepsis after loss of splenic function.
questions.why: Repeated splenic infarction from sickling leaves most children with HbSS functionally asplenic in early childhood, shown here by Howell-Jolly bodies and a nonpalpable spleen. Marginal zone B cells and macrophages of the spleen make IgM against capsular polysaccharides and remove opsonized encapsulated bacteria from the blood. Without them, encapsulated organisms such as S pneumoniae, H influenzae type b, and N meningitidis can cause rapidly fatal sepsis. S pneumoniae is the most common cause, which is why these children receive daily penicillin and pneumococcal vaccines.
whyNot: Pseudomonas aeruginosa causes serious infection with neutropenia, burns, cystic fibrosis, and hospital devices. Asplenia is not its main risk factor.
Correct.
Staphylococcus epidermidis infects catheters and prosthetic devices through biofilm. It is not a typical cause of postsplenectomy sepsis.
Listeria monocytogenes is an intracellular organism controlled by cell-mediated immunity. It threatens neonates, pregnant women, older adults, and people with T cell defects.
